title: Public-life participation is segmented into mobilizers, connectors, spectators, and outsiders rather than one engagement scale
source_unit: Pew Research Center and Pew-Knight Initiative Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey and American Trends Panel analysis

observations.period: July 9 to December 5, 2025; public-life engagement typology published July 2026

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew's Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey; group percentages exclude adults not assigned to a group

mobilizers.unit: percent of U.S. adults categorized in the highest cross-domain engagement group

connectors.unit: percent of U.S. adults categorized as community-, charitable-, religious-, and voting-oriented participants with less political action

spectators.unit: percent of U.S. adults categorized as news-attentive but less civically or politically active

outsiders.unit: percent of U.S. adults categorized as relatively low across measured news, civic, political, and religious activities

unassigned.value: The displayed groups do not sum to 100% because respondents who were not categorized are not shown

observations.method: Pew used cluster analysis on 19 measures of political activity, civic involvement, religious attendance, and attention to news. The main cross-sectional survey offered online, paper, and telephone response modes and made multiple contact attempts; the source states that the typology is a one-time late-2025 picture rather than a time-series trend.
observations.uncertainty: The groups are analytical classifications, not fixed identities or levels of civic virtue. They depend on selected questions, clustering choices, recent political-cycle timing, nonresponse, and the decision not to display unassigned respondents. The survey does not show causal pathways from news, religion, income, or technology to participation.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults assigned to four cross-domain engagement groups; the typology is not respondent-level data in this record.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low measured participation can coexist with episodic voting, informal care, private discussion, or activities outside the 19 measures. A large spectator or outsider share does not by itself establish political apathy or democratic decline.

observations.period: July 9 to December 5, 2025; engagement-group behavior profiles

denominator.unit: Pew engagement-group estimate; percentages are within-group reported behavior shares

voted_2024.unit: percent within each group reporting voting in 2024

contacted_elected_official.unit: percent within each group reporting contact with an elected official in the past year

volunteered.unit: percent within each group reporting volunteering in the past year

follow_national_news.unit: percent within each group following national news at least somewhat closely

political_mixture.value: Each group contains both Republicans and Democrats; no engagement group is dominated by one party

observations.method: Pew compared reported behaviors across the four clusters and used Wave 179 of the American Trends Panel, conducted September 8-14, 2025 among 5,195 respondents, to examine political views and civic knowledge. The article reports group-level percentages and does not claim that group membership causes behavior.
observations.uncertainty: All measures are self-reported and many cover the prior 12 months, a period that included the 2024 presidential election. The cross-sectional design cannot establish persistence, sequence, or causal effects; similar group averages can conceal substantial within-group variation.
observations.subgroup: Mobilizers, Connectors, Spectators, and Outsiders, with comparisons across voting, contacting officials, volunteering, news attention, religious attendance, donations, and partisan composition.
observations.counterinterpretation: Engagement may be episodic and context-dependent; outsiders still include people who voted, attended religious services, or acted outside the measured channels. Political mixture within groups means participation style is not reducible to party identity.

boundary: This record adds a cross-domain public-life participation typology linking news attention, political action, civic involvement, religious participation, and voting. It does not infer civic health, democratic legitimacy, political causality, stable identities, or individual-level respondent behavior beyond Pew's aggregate group estimates.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Pew publication HTML retrieved; publication date, survey samples, cluster dimensions, four-group shares, behavior comparisons, partisan mixture, and stated classification/time-period boundaries cross-checked against the page.
